extracted.intended_audience: manuscript editors, copyeditors, production editors, and authors preparing book- or journal-length manuscripts (including self-published authors)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and standards for preparing, copyediting, and readying book- and article-length manuscripts for production, including front/back matter, markup, author communication, and electronic cleanup. Covers editorial decision rules, mechanical procedures, and production checklist items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing front matter
rubrics_metrics.description: An editor should check any half title, title page, table of contents, and list of illustrations against the text and captions and against any applicable documentation included with the manuscript; discrepancies should be queried.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If subheads are to be dropped from the table of contents, consult the author. For books, pay attention to the order of elements and label the manuscript to ensure correct roman numeral pagination. Publishers generally prepare the copyright page, though editors may review the author’s biographical note and other elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing part titles and chapter/article titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure that part and chapter titles and their subtitles, if any, are consistent with the text in spelling, hyphenation, and italics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chicago recommends headline-style capitalization for titles unless a series or journal uses another style. Check each title against the table of contents and query discrepancies. Identify titles on the manuscript per publisher requirements (see electronic vs paper manuscript sections).

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing subheads
rubrics_metrics.description: Subheads should be checked for consistency with the text in spelling, hyphenation, and italics, and for parallel structure and tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust the text immediately following a subhead for proper wording relative to the subhead. Verify hierarchy if more than one subhead level; clearly identify each level and consider eliminating the lowest level if there are more than three. For electronic manuscripts, apply appropriate markup for subhead levels early to preserve typographic distinctions. If subheads are to appear in the table of contents, cross-check for consistency. Respect an author’s consistently applied sentence-style subheads unless consulted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing cross-references
rubrics_metrics.description: All references to tables, figures, appendixes, bibliographies, or other parts of a work should be checked by the manuscript editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point out discrepancies (e.g., a reference to 2017 data when the table gives 2016). Minimize or eliminate cross-references to specific pages because pagination may change; ensure place-names on maps match text spelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing quotations and previously published material
rubrics_metrics.description: Do nothing to quoted material except to adjust punctuation to house style unless translating or modernizing, in which case light editing may be done; transcribed interviews/field notes may be edited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Query misspelled words and apparent transcription errors; ask authors who appear careless in transcribing to recheck quotations for accuracy, including punctuation. Ensure sources are given for all quoted material. When editing previously published or abridged material, read for sense to ensure nothing is out of order or omitted and query discrepancies. Clarify ambiguous end-of-line hyphens from paper-supplied material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing notes (footnotes and endnotes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each note must be checked against the text to ensure that its text reference is correct and in the right place and that any terms used in the note are treated the same way as in the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask authors to shorten excessively long notes or to incorporate note material into the text when printing as footnotes. Place lists, tables, and figures in the text or an appendix, not in footnotes. Editors may request additional notes or combine/delete notes in consultation with the author. Take special care when renumbering notes in paper editing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing note citations, bibliographies, and reference lists
rubrics_metrics.description: Citations in notes, bibliographies, and reference lists must be carefully checked for documentation style; subsequent references must match the first-reference form or the accepted shortened form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In works containing both bibliography and notes, check each citation in notes against the bibliography and resolve discrepancies or query in both contexts. Bibliographies should be checked for alphabetical (and where applicable chronological) order. For author-date styles, check all text citations against the reference list. Editors working on-screen should ensure source citations are free of underlying codes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility in style for source citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Imposing house style on notes prepared in another consistent and clear style can be time-consuming and often unnecessary, especially for standalone books.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before making sweeping changes to citation style, consult the author or publisher. In journal editing, flexibility is usually not allowed because citations are often linked to resources and require a consistent predictable format across articles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing illustrations and captions
rubrics_metrics.description: Wording in diagrams, charts, maps, and the like should generally conform to the spelling and capitalization used in captions or the text; captions must conform to the style of the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Edit source information in consultation with the publisher and in conformance with letters of permission. If permissions are outstanding, the publisher should handle them. Illustrations may be added, dropped, or renumbered; make a final check of all illustrations against text references and the list of illustrations to ensure they match and show what they claim. See separate guidance for preparing illustrations and checking credits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing tables
rubrics_metrics.description: Tables are usually best edited together as a group to ensure consistent style and presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check tables for consistent numbering and correspondence with the text, including text references and placement callouts. Follow specific table-editing guidelines referenced elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing indexes
rubrics_metrics.description: The schedule for editing an index must usually correspond to the schedule for reviewing corrections to proofs, since page-number locators are determined late.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow detailed index-editing checklist and timing guidance; index preparation is typically done after composition/typesetting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contacting the author after an initial review
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors of book-length works are urged to contact their authors early on after an initial review, especially if there are questions or planned significant changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early contact is important in case the author is unamenable to changes that would be costly to undo. Notify authors of systematic changes to expedite production. Authors’ wishes should generally be respected unless usage is determined by journal or series style. For extensive changes, consider sending a sample of the editing for author approval before proceeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing author comments and queries
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors may impose consistent style and correct obvious errors without comment; corrections to less obvious problems may warrant concise queries that avoid sounding casual, pedantic, condescending, or indignant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple yes/no queries (e.g., “OK?”) are often enough. For non-yes/no issues, be specific—e.g., 'Do you mean X or Y?' Examples of when to query include noting a silent global correction, pointing out discrepancies in spellings or citations, apparent omissions or quote errors, repetition, verification of hard-to-check names/terms, clarification of ambiguous text, and citing sources consulted in correcting factual errors (with cautions about revealing sources). See mechanics sections for entering queries on electronic and paper manuscripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanics for entering queries (electronic and paper)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are recommended practices for entering queries on electronic manuscripts (see 2.87) and on paper manuscripts (see 2.92).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the word processor’s commenting feature for queries in electronic manuscripts and follow the established procedures for marking queries on paper manuscripts; see the detailed referenced sections for the mechanics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing a cover letter to the author
rubrics_metrics.description: The letter sent with the edited manuscript should explain the nature and scope of the editing and provide instructions and reminders to the author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include items such as: nature/scope of edits; how edits are shown (tracking or pencil) and instructions to interpret marks; how the author should respond to queries and veto edits; warning that author review is the last opportunity for substantive changes and a reminder to check quoted matter/citations; reminder to retain a copy; deadline for return; discussion about the index and who will prepare it; request for confirmation of contact information and availability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sending the edited manuscript to the author
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose an appropriate mode (hard copy/PDF or electronic) for the author's review, considering manuscript length and complexity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Book-length edited manuscripts may be sent as hard copy or as a PDF to print; authors mark a printout and return it to the editor who incorporates marks. Alternatively, authors may review the electronic manuscript using the same software (saves printing/shipping) but the editor must ensure authors do not make undocumented changes—strategies include locking the document so changes are visibly tracked. For article-length works, authors may annotate a PDF on-screen. Pencil-edited manuscripts should be scanned/photocopied before sending; both editors and authors should keep copies because pencil-edited pages can be unique and irreplaceable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checking the author's review of the edited manuscript
rubrics_metrics.description: When the manuscript returns from the author, the editor must check that all queries have been answered and edit any new material; update electronic files or clarify/retype new handwritten material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the author has rewritten extensively, another editing pass and author review may be needed. Except for style adjustments, the author’s version should prevail; seek compromise if unacceptable. Cross out queries when updating paper copies and ensure electronic files are updated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensuring correct markup
rubrics_metrics.description: Double-check that each component part of the manuscript has been properly identified in the final edited manuscript according to the system of markup used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For a book, parts include title, table of contents, chapters, sections, subheads, extracts, lists, notes, illustrations/captions, tables, etc. Also check character-level markup (italics, cross-references that will be hyperlinked). Manuscript editors are usually responsible for initial checking of markup because they are closest to the content; once in production, markup responsibility typically passes to the production department. Self-published authors must be aware of formatting/submission guidelines from their platform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type specifications and hand markup
rubrics_metrics.description: An editor may need to hand-mark hard copy with appropriate type specifications at the first occurrence of elements to apply to the manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: margin notes indicating 'text: 10/12 Times Roman x 26' or 'extract: 9/11 Times Roman; indent 2 pi from left.' If extracts are labeled 'ext' and first-level subheads 'A,' markup can be minimized. See hand-markup procedure references for more details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensuring correct pagination
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicate where roman page numbers are to end and arabic numbers begin and ensure all elements are in correct order as reflected in the table of contents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify where a part or chapter should start (e.g., whether elements begin on recto or verso). Repagination of typeset books is expensive, so check front matter, text, and back matter order carefully. For journals, follow journal-specific rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparing running heads
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide suggested copy for running heads (or feet) and indicate which heads belong on versos and which on rectos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Running heads must fit on a single line (usually with the page number), so chapter titles may need shortening while retaining key terms. For some languages, retain words that govern case endings. Send running-head copy to the author if author approval may be needed. Include running-head copy with other electronic files to the typesetter. If running heads reflect particular pages, determine exact copy after or as pages are typeset. For electronic formats, specify short forms (alt-title) in the markup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production checklist (vital statistics to accompany ready-to-typeset manuscripts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts ready for typesetting should be accompanied by a checklist of vital project and production information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Checklist items may include: author name and title; list of component parts (electronic files, printout, illustrations); details about software used and file names; list of markup labels/styles and any special characters/fonts; list of outstanding material; indication of how notes are to be set (footnotes vs endnotes); list of front/text/end-matter elements and which must start recto; for book-length works, who will receive page proofs and in what format.

rubrics_metrics.name: Saving manuscript files and keeping backups
rubrics_metrics.description: Save and back up a manuscript in stages, creating separate copies of each significant version; archive the author's original and every significant stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Name stages distinctly (e.g., 'author’s original', 'clean unedited', 'first edit', 'to author'), use different directories for complex projects, save frequently while editing, and back up all saved versions to a second location. Use file-hosting services that allow access to previous versions as an additional safeguard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript cleanup tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Use word-processor tools and third-party add-ins to automate repetitive cleanup tasks (search-and-replace, pattern matching, macros) when preparing electronic files for editing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers may supply cleaned-up files and specify software/markup. If editors must clean up files themselves, learn pattern matching, macros, and available add-ins. Consult word-processor help for instructions and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript cleanup checklist (preediting electronic cleanup)
rubrics_metrics.description: A suggested set of steps to prepare electronic files for editing; not all steps apply to every manuscript and the order may be adapted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Checklist items (summarized): convert files for the publisher’s editing software; consider combining separate files into one complete manuscript; change language settings if necessary; scroll through the whole manuscript with formatting/markup displayed to fix conversion errors; identify graphic elements and handle appropriately; apply markup for elements whose visual cues may be lost; delete extraneous spaces/tabs and replace multiple-space indents with tabs/software indents; change multiple hard returns to single; change underlining to italics (preserve true underscore when required and note exceptions); fix quotation marks and apostrophes (taking account of transliteration uses); fix commas/periods relative to quotation marks; regularize em dashes and ellipses; replace hyphens between numerals with en dashes as appropriate; convert footnotes to endnotes or vice versa; delete optional/conditional hyphens; correct l/1 and o/0 confusions using pattern matching; fix other global inconsistencies (e.g., spaced initials); adjust line spacing, font, and margins as desired; and finally save a copy of the clean, unedited manuscript.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic markup for electronic manuscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Each element of a manuscript must be identified using consistent markup labels (generic or formal) so they can be systematically identified and replaced for publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use labels (e.g., ..., ..., ..., ...) enclosed in delimiters and applied at the beginning and end of elements. Publishers differ in what elements they require marked up. Consistency and accuracy are crucial; supply a complete list of markup with the manuscript. End tags may be unnecessary for single-paragraph elements depending on requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word-processing styles
rubrics_metrics.description: Use word-processor templates with paragraph and character styles defined for a manuscript so editors/authors can work in familiar software while facilitating production markup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paragraph-level style names should be descriptive of the element (e.g., 'chapter number', 'A-head') rather than appearance; character-level styles should specify intent ('emphasis' not 'italic'). Define appropriate formatting attributes for each style to facilitate editing and author review. Accuracy and consistency in applying styles is more important than the formatting itself. Annotated list of styles should accompany the manuscript. Authors reviewing edited manuscripts should be advised not to modify styles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal markup languages and tagging structure (e.g., XML)
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts may need conversion and tagging according to rules of formal markup languages like XML for e-books, web presentation, or apps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use word-processing styles mapped to tags to facilitate conversion. Tags are paired and nested to reflect document structure; tagging is structural and semantic (identify what an element is, not how it should look). Tags may also denote functional elements (e.g., hyperlinked cross-references or emphasized terms). Presentation details are specified in style sheets per format. If editing after conversion to formal markup, the editor should help ensure tags are applied correctly. Implementing such workflows requires significant technical expertise. Note: semantic character-level markup improves accessibility for assistive technologies; consult WAI/W3C and EPUB accessibility guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tracking changes (redlining)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a word processor’s change-tracking feature to show edits so authors can see additions and deletions and to facilitate review; insert author queries using commenting features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With tracking on, added text is underlined and deletions struck through (display depends on software). Include explanatory comments for ambiguous or hard-to-interpret changes; avoid making changes that might be missed—when in doubt, strike out the entire term and replace it. Ensure legibility in black-and-white printouts and use comments for first occurrences of global changes. See also guidance for marking changes on PDF files.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making silent changes (not tracking) and when to track globals
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether to track all mechanical and substantive edits; some editors turn off tracking for mechanical global changes to avoid distracting authors, but should alert the author that such global changes were made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A common practice is to track only the first instance of a global change and insert a comment alerting the author that subsequent instances were changed silently. The decision depends on editor/publisher preferences and what will best serve author-review clarity.
